html:
The Western Deffufa is a huge mud-brick temple at Kerma in northern Sudan, near the Third Cataract of the Nile. Begun around 2500 BCE and rebuilt many times, it still stands about 18 metres high, among the oldest and largest buildings in Africa south of Egypt.

Kerma was the capital of the first great kingdom of Nubia, which grew rich on trade in gold, ivory and cattle and was a rival of Egypt for centuries. The deffufa was a solid mass of brick with a narrow stair inside leading to a shrine on top. Around it lay workshops, storerooms and houses. A second building, the Eastern Deffufa, stood by the royal cemetery, where kings were buried with hundreds of sacrificed followers.

Egypt of the New Kingdom conquered Kerma around 1500 BCE under Thutmose I. Later Nubian power rose again in Kush. The site was dug by George Reisner in the 1910s and by a Swiss team under Charles Bonnet from the 1970s.
